## Solution

We evaluate
$$I = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{\ln\!\left(x+\frac{1}{x}\right)}{1+x^2}\,dx.$$

**Convergence.** Near $x\to 0^+$, $x+\frac1x\sim \frac1x$, so the integrand $\sim -\ln x$, which is integrable on $(0,1)$. Near $x\to\infty$, $x+\frac1x\sim x$ and $\frac{1}{1+x^2}\sim x^{-2}$, so the integrand $\sim \frac{\ln x}{x^2}$, integrable on $(1,\infty)$. Hence $I$ converges.

**Substitution.** Set $x=\tan\theta$, so $dx=\sec^2\theta\,d\theta$ and $1+x^2=\sec^2\theta$, giving $\frac{dx}{1+x^2}=d\theta$. As $x:0\to\infty$, $\theta:0\to\frac\pi2$. Thus
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\!\left(\tan\theta+\cot\theta\right)d\theta.$$

**Simplify the logarithm.** Using $\tan\theta+\cot\theta=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}+\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\frac{\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\frac{1}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}=\frac{2}{\sin 2\theta}$,
$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\!\left(\frac{2}{\sin 2\theta}\right)d\theta=\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2-\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin 2\theta)\,d\theta.$$

**Reduce to the classical integral.** Let $u=2\theta$, $du=2\,d\theta$:
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin 2\theta)\,d\theta=\frac12\int_0^{\pi}\ln(\sin u)\,du=\frac12\cdot 2\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin u)\,du=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin u)\,du,$$
where we used the symmetry $\sin(\pi-u)=\sin u$.

**Evaluate the classical integral.** Let $J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin u)\,du$. By $u\mapsto \frac\pi2-u$, also $J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\cos u)\,du$. Hence
$$2J=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin u\cos u)\,du=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln\!\left(\frac{\sin 2u}{2}\right)du=\int_0^{\pi/2}\ln(\sin 2u)\,du-\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2.$$
The remaining integral equals $\frac12\int_0^\pi\ln(\sin v)\,dv=J$ by the same substitution/symmetry as above. Therefore
$$2J=J-\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad J=-\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2.$$

**Combine.**
$$I=\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2-J=\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2-\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}\ln 2\right)=\pi\ln 2.$$

$$\boxed{\,I=\pi\ln 2\,}$$

### PROOF COMPLETE
